[01] / MA Dissertation / ARTD6241 / Winchester School of Art / 2026

THE LOCALIZATION PLAYBOOK

Six European heritage houses, two Gulf markets, and the point where adapting for a region quietly turns into borrowing its look.

The question

Kapferer and Bastien's anti-laws of luxury say a house shouldn't bend too far for one market. The Gulf is testing that. I followed Louis Vuitton, Chanel, Dior, Cartier, Bvlgari and Hermès from January 2022 to June 2026: their Instagram, plus their stores, launches and ambassadors in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

What I found

Across 9,625 posts and 131,407 comments, I couldn't find a single caption or hashtag written in Arabic. The Arabic was all in the comments: 1,431 of them, appearing under 21.6% of Cartier's posts alone. The audience is clearly there, talking in its own language. Nothing comes back.

All six adapt somehow. What varies is how much they're willing to show. Chanel opened a 538 square metre twin boutique in Riyadh in 2025 and its 1,808 posts never mention a Gulf city, Ramadan or Eid. Louis Vuitton launched Mirage for the Gulf in January 2026, posted 67 times that month and never named it. Bvlgari turns up for Ramadan year after year.

Talking to Riyadh and talking to the world while Riyadh watches can look identical on a feed. They are different decisions.

The framework

That gap became Audience Direction, a matrix that asks two things of every post: how far does the adaptation go, and who is it actually for?

The data showed no obvious commercial penalty for borrowing a region's look without addressing the region, so I wouldn't pitch Arabic on the main feed as a revenue win. I'd argue it on respect, and on Vision 2030 favouring brands that build locally over brands that fly campaigns in.

Keeping it honest

My manual count gave Cartier 17 Gulf-directed posts and the automated pass gave 9, enough to change whether Cartier or Bvlgari comes out on top, so I reported both. As a Pakistani Muslim I notice straight away when a campaign lines up with Ramadan, which cuts both ways: it's easy to over-read a brand's effort, or to credit it just for trying.

[02] / CRM & Marketing Automation Consultant / BAAM, New York (remote) / 2025 to now

CRM & AUTOMATION

The unglamorous half of luxury: knowing who a client is, what they want next, and making sure nobody has to remember to follow up.

The work

At BAAM I provide marketing consultancy and CRM implementation on GoHighLevel and HubSpot, supporting client acquisition and campaign management. Day to day that means mapping customer journeys, optimising funnels, segmenting audiences on real data, and building the automation behind enterprise onboarding and ongoing client engagement.

What goes into a flow

  1. Map the journey. Every touchpoint from first enquiry to repeat client, and where people drop off.
  2. Segment on data. Tag contacts by source, interest and value, so nobody gets a message meant for someone else.
  3. Automate the follow-up. Triggers, conditions and timed email and SMS sequences that move people forward without anyone chasing them.
  4. Onboard properly. Welcome, documents, reminders and hand-offs, so the first week feels considered rather than administrative.
  5. Keep engagement going. Campaigns that keep existing clients close long after the first sale.
A great client advisor remembers your name, your size and your anniversary. A great CRM makes sure that survives staff turnover.

Why it matters in luxury

Clienteling is a CRM discipline wearing a nicer suit. The thinking that keeps an enterprise onboarding flow on track is the same thinking that lets a boutique know a client's preferences before they walk in. It's also why my research leans on data at scale: the dissertation worked through 131,407 comments.

[03] / The Business of Luxury / Group consultancy / Report + pitch deck

BREMONT 2027

Taking a British watchmaker to the US on culture, because on specs alone it was never going to win.

The brief

Bremont briefed us to build the marketing strategy for its 2027 US expansion. The product wasn't the problem: the Terra Nova competes well on credibility and aviation heritage. But with weaker specs than Tudor and Longines, it had to win on culture, not just craftsmanship.

The real challenge was reshaping how Bremont connects with people, not simply promoting a new collection.

Three acts, £3.2M

  • 001The Exhibit. Guerrilla installations at Heathrow, JFK, Grand Central and Waterloo, pairing war-era aircraft with the Terra Nova to build heritage visibility and earned media.
  • 002The Collective. A travelling pop-up across New York, Miami, Dallas and LA, putting Bremont alongside Aston Martin, Hackett, Crockett & Jones and Globe-Trotter in one British luxury ecosystem.
  • 003The Wayfinder Weekends. An ambassador-led outdoor membership programme to turn one-time visitors into a community that stays.

My part

I led creative direction on The Collective and pushed for a cinematic, slightly Bond-inspired tone across the visuals. Biggest lesson: a strong creative idea only gets you halfway. The other half is defending it, which is where Pine & Gilmore's Experience Economy and Moore's brand ecosystems did the heavy lifting.

[04] / Exploring the Visual Language of Display / Retail display concept

HANA TO HEIWA

A six-day display for Tokyo's oldest department store, where the most important object is the one that isn't there.

The concept

Hana to Heiwa, flowers and peace, runs at Mitsukoshi Nihonbashi for six days between Hinamatsuri on 3 March and International Women's Day on 8 March 2027. The brief was to treat display as language: not just what it looks like, but what it says. This one makes a quiet argument about women and leadership in Japan, using architecture, routing and product curation instead of slogans.

Display is treated as a message, not décor.

Inside

  • 01A 4m hinadan beneath the historic 1930 pipe organ, with the Empress doll set at equal height to the Emperor. A small, deliberate shift.
  • 02A night-time façade projection that turns the whole building into a living hinadan.
  • 03A tsurushi-bina corridor: the passage from cosmetics to jewellery becomes a ceiling of fabric dolls, paper cranes and cherry blossom.
  • 04A Leadership Gallery ending at an empty plinth labelled 2027 and Mirai. After Baudrillard, the missing object is the statement.
  • 05Floor staff as storytellers rather than salespeople, and a stamp card that takes visitors through the whole store to complete a portrait of Japanese women's history.

Around it: collaborations with Issey Miyake, Mikimoto and Wajima lacquerware, a PR campaign across Tokyo Metro and Vogue Japan, and styling for 80 floor staff.

[05] / Professional Luxury Practices / Business report

FABERGÉ / TSAR'S JEWEL

A recovery plan for a house whose imperial mystique is both its best asset and its heaviest luggage.

The problem

Goldsmith to the Russian Imperial Court, the Easter Eggs, a century of heritage. Then a revolution, decades of changing owners, and by the time Gemfields bought it in 2013 the issue wasn't awareness. It was confusion. People genuinely asked: is this the real Fabergé?

The 2024 numbers held a contradiction. Fabergé became financially self-sufficient within Gemfields for the first time, yet revenue fell 15% to $13.4M with $5.7M in operating losses. Harrods closed and 2023's one-off legacy sales didn't repeat. Strip those out and the brand actually grew 2%.

Three pillars, 2026 to 2030

  • IOperational optimisation. Free up capital by moving $15M of trapped showpiece inventory through private sales and auctions.
  • IIBrand clarity reset. An "Imperial House Reborn" campaign, anchored by the new Piccadilly boutique and private client salons in Dubai and potentially New York.
  • IIIProduct and experiential innovation. Contemporary commissions from $500K to $5M, blockchain-enabled provenance through Gemfields, and annual Heritage editions in fully traceable Mozambican rubies and Zambian emeralds.
Legacy alone doesn't protect you. If your story gets fragmented, even a name like Fabergé becomes a liability.

The edge nobody else in high jewellery has: a mine-to-market supply chain. LVMH and Richemont dominate the category, but every Fabergé stone can be traced to its source, which matters more each year to younger HNWIs who judge luxury on values rather than status.

[06] / Principles of Luxury / Brand creation

THE CAGLIOSTRO UNIVERSE

A luxury cigar house, built from nothing, that tells you less on purpose.

The brief

Create a luxury brand from scratch: not a name and a logo but a full ecosystem, with brand rationale, website, Instagram strategy and a mini brand film. I built a cigar house named after Count Alessandro di Cagliostro, the 18th-century magician who held European high society spellbound. Tagline: For Those Who Command the Room.

The thinking

Kapferer's anti-laws shaped the positioning. Instead of chasing reach, a digital velvet rope controls access and engineers scarcity, borrowing from De Beers' playbook. While most of luxury rushes towards transparency, Cagliostro withholds on purpose: Athwal and Wells call it maintaining the dream. Habanos and Davidoff win on presence, so Cagliostro goes the other way.

Bourdieu's idea of polyhedric identity holds it together: the same client is a different person in the boardroom, at leisure and in culture, and the brand meets all of them without fragmenting.

In luxury, what you don't show matters more than what you do.

What I made

  • 01A website where the call to action is "Discovery", reframing browsing as a journey, with store locations treated as a privilege.
  • 02Humidors in individually numbered burl walnut with sterling silver inlays, positioned as collectible art rather than storage.
  • 03A shadow-rich Instagram plan that keeps well clear of shallow glamour.
  • 04A brand film opening on New York at night, cut to cigar-cutter clicks and live jazz, with no voiceover and no logo until the final frame.

[07] / ARTD6144 The Context of Luxury / Academic essay

WHY IS LUXURY A CONTESTED ISSUE?

From Beau Brummell to Virgil Abloh: who gets to define luxury, and who gets quietly shown the door.

The argument

Luxury isn't a category of goods. It's a symbolic system that reproduces, disrupts and renegotiates social hierarchy. Using Bourdieu's habitus, cultural capital and symbolic violence, the essay follows distinction in menswear from Beau Brummell and the Teddy Boys to now.

It reads Gen Z's value-led identity, the geographic shift in luxury spending and Virgil Abloh's "zeroing" at Louis Vuitton as disruptions to the old story, with Abloh both inside and outside the establishment.

Can you perform indifference convincingly? Not many can, because the nonchalance comes from privilege itself.FROM THE ESSAY

Then it turns on quiet luxury. Dropping the logo is still a status signal, just a higher-order one. The code shifts the moment you learn it.
